title: The normalize loop pair
hints: Two loops, like the rendered C: one for the reduce, one for the store. The scalar between them (the reciprocal) is computed once, after the first loop.

Fold strictly left to right: `s = x[0]`, then `s = s + x[1]`, and so on. f32 addition isn't associative, so adding `1` to `1e8` five times gives `1e8`, while `1e8 + (1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1)` gives `100000008`.
`x[i] / s` and `x[i] * (1.0f / s)` round differently for some inputs. The program says `mul` by `recip`, so multiply by a precomputed `1.0f / s`.
explain: This is the C a rangeified renderer produces for `x * expand(recip(sum(x)))`: the reduce becomes a loop seeded with `x[0]`, the reciprocal is a scalar hoisted between the loops, and the store loop multiplies. Dividing instead of multiplying by the reciprocal gives different bits for inputs like {-2.5, 3, 2, 5}, which is why the grader's bit-for-bit comparison catches it.

tests.expr: ({ float x[4] = {1.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f, 4.0f}; float y[4]; normalize(x, y, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &y[3], 4); u; })
({ float x[4] = {-2.5f, 3.0f, 2.0f, 5.0f}; float y[4]; normalize(x, y, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &y[1], 4); u; })
({ float x[4] = {-2.5f, 3.0f, 7.0f, 0.3f}; float y[4]; normalize(x, y, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &y[2], 4); u; })
({ float x[4] = {-2.5f, 3.0f, 7.0f, 0.3f}; float y[4]; normalize(x, y, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &y[3], 4); u; })
({ float x[4] = {1.0f, 5.0f, 0.001f, -2.5f}; float y[4]; normalize(x, y, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &y[1], 4); u; })
({ float x[4] = {100000000.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f}; float y[4]; normalize(x, y, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &y[3], 4); u; })
